SAMANTHA: [She doesn't mention her job]
5987:
Transcription

[What do you like about London?]

KEVIN: There are people from all over the world here. It’s fascinating. I love to go to different parts of the city, listen to the strange music coming from the shops, and go to an international restaurant and try something that I can’t pronounce!
SAMANTHA: There are so many different events here. Ballet, theatre, arts projects, festivals, carnivals… you can see dance and music styles from all over the world. You can’t experience that back in my home town.
5988:
Transcription

[What do you dislike about it?]

KEVIN: Nothing. People say London is expensive, but I manage to live cheaply. I share a room with an Australian guy, I cycle everywhere, I buy cheap food and I get a lot of clothes and things for my flat free, because people are giving them away. People say there’s a lot of crime too, but I haven’t experienced anything myself – let’s hope that continues!
SAMANTHA: Well, I haven’t had any problems personally, but I guess I am always aware that this is a big city and crimes happen, so I’m never completely relaxed. Everything costs a fortune too: my accommodation, food, transport, bars, restaurants and events. I wish I earned more. Then I would be able to experience more that this city can offer.

Let me see. I’ve worked here for four years now, but for one year, I commuted into Brighton by train. But after that, I got a room in a shared house in Brighton, and I lived there for a year before I got my own flat here two years ago.
6001:
Transcription

Lots of people like Brighton because it’s on the coast, but I grew up by the sea so that’s nothing special for me. There’s always plenty going on though. Festivals, shows, sports events. I like that. My friends say the nightlife is good too, but I don’t go out to bars much, so I wouldn’t know.
6002:
Transcription

My things are always getting stolen! two bikes, a bag, two phones. And recently I read about someone who was attacked just after getting off the bus stop outside my flat! It’s a shame, because most people are really friendly and care about the city. It used to be a really dirty place, but volunteers do a great job cleaning it up.
6003:

Well I used to cycle everywhere, but since my last bike was taken 18 months ago, I’ve used a skateboard instead. I can carry it into shops with me, or into the office. If I need to, I can take it on the bus. I don’t drive. None of my friends do, because it’s so hard to find places to park a car.

Transcription

Well, there are lots of great restaurants in the city, but I think my favourite place to eat out is a little café. It is on the edge of town, three of four miles from the city centre. It’s on the beach, on the other side of the harbour. I go there in the mornings before work for a coffee and a bacon roll. It’s a great start to the day before I go to the office.

Well my first best friend was Kevin. We’ve known each other since we were babies.
6007:
Transcription

My mum and his made friends at those classes that women go to when they are pregnant. They both went swimming together before Kevin and I were born. Our mums always hung out when we were babies and so we did too.
6008:
Transcription

At primary school, we were always together. We were both smart so we could always sit together in class.
6009:
Transcription

In our free time, we used to play computer games and watch war movies. We both hated sports.

He started going to the gym too, which never interested me. I joined a board games club and met new friends there, but we were never as close as Kevin and I had been. I’ve only seen him a couple of times since high school. He moved to Dubai and got married.
6013:
Transcription

At university, I made friends with a housemate called Charlie. He’s completely different from me. I’m quite quiet, but he is really noisy, chatty, friendly and crazy.
6014:
Transcription

He opened up my world, introducing me to night clubs, rock concerts, beach holidays. I used to wonder why he liked me – he was so sociable and I was so serious. But I later found out that his family life had been very difficult as a kid. I was honest and reliable, and his parents were not.
6015:
Transcription

After university, Charlie and I got jobs in different cities and saw less of each other. We both had serious relationships, but we both broke up at about the same time. To get over it, the two of us went on holiday together. We had a really good time, and after that, Charlie quit his job and moved to my city.
6018:
Transcription

Now we hang out at least once a week. We usually play computer games or go to a bar. He wants me to play racquetball with him, but I’m not interested in that.

6024:
Transcription

KATE: Do you enjoy it?
DANIEL: Not really. I miss chatting to people, joking around, or deciding at the last minute to go for a drink or dinner after work. Just chatting to colleagues, we found things we had in common.
6025:
Transcription

6026:
Transcription

6027:
Transcription

Transcription

Transcription

Now, the kids are older, so after some discussion, my wife agreed I could get a job I loved, even though I will be home much later, and earn less. I started last week. It’s great!

It’s not easy, but now we spend a lot more time together and it’s good for all of us.

Transcription

6041:
Transcription

6042:
Transcription

Transcription

Well, I guess my favourite kind of movie is sci-fi. If I’m at home in the evening, and I want to watch a film, that’s the first kind of film I will look for. I think those films are imaginative and interesting. However, there are some terrible sci-fi films out there! But even the terrible ones are funny, sometimes!
6340:
Transcription

Rom-coms, uurgh no. I don’t watch those unless I have to. My girlfriend loves them and sometimes I watch them if we are having a romantic evening at home. But they are so boring and predictable. The characters are always the same. They are rarely funny.
6341:
Transcription

I like horror films, though. They are predictable, I know, but I just enjoy them. I often watch them with friends and we try to guess what is going to happen, so it’s always sociable. It’s also interesting to discuss how they did the special effects and horrible make-up. I used to think horror films were scary, but now I don’t.
6342:
Transcription

I love animated films too. All kinds, from Japanese anime to children’s cartoons. I think the Japanese style films are really beautiful, creative and imaginative. The stories are strange, but the artwork is beautiful. And some children’s cartoons are really funny. I watch them with my little cousin. There is something for everyone, kids and adults.
6343:
Transcription

I used to love action films, but I don’t think modern action films are as good as the ones in the past. Before, they were big-budget, blockbuster films. They were set in amazing locations and the stunts were incredible. Now they are often low-budget with lots of computer graphics. They just aren’t as exciting.
6344:
Transcription

I don’t often watch documentaries. I suppose in the evenings, I don’t want to learn. I want to relax. And many documentaries are depressing. They tell you about all the things that are bad in the world. It’s important information, but those kinds of films aren’t very enjoyable.
6345:
Transcription

And musicals! I hate them! I can’t understand why people are talking and then they start singing! Of course, musicals aren’t very popular now, like they were in the past, and that’s a good thing! My girlfriend loves them, but luckily, she prefers to watch them with her friends and they sing along together. I don’t have to watch!

INTERVIEWER: Is salary a deciding factor when choosing a job?
TOBY: I remember at school years ago, we always used to say that the amount of money you earn is unimportant and that it's better to have an interesting job as long as you get a fair wage. Well, that's just it, isn't it? When I started looking at how much these interesting jobs pay and the number of unpaid hours you are expected to do, it's just not enough to live on. So, I've changed my tune now. I'm not prepared to work for next to nothing.
7289:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Would you be willing to work longer hours if you were asked to?
TOBY: There's only so much I'm prepared to do. I have friends who work all the hours god sends, thinking all those extra hours will earn them recognition in the company and get them a promotion. I'm not convinced that it gets them anywhere, and they don't have much of a life outside of work. I'd rather maintain a decent work-life balance.

INTERVIEWER: How important is flexibility?
TOBY: Very important. I'm sure everyone would agree. It's impossible to raise children, see a doctor or care for your elderly relatives with most jobs. I remember when we left school, we were all eager to meet up at a reunion ten twenty years down the line. We said we'd want to see how we've changed, but let's face it, we were all looking forward to a chance to brag about our achievements. That doesn't appeal to me anymore, nor do I really care about hanging out with people from my past. I've kept up with the ones I really care about. I was more curious about the place itself. It had always been so old-fashioned. I wondered if it had remained that way or moved on.
7361:
Transcription

At first, the atmosphere was rather awkward. I paired off with a close friend, Emily, and we updated each other on life. Around us, some people were squealing with joy as they met long-lost friends and reminiscing, while others who had come and then realised they didn't know anyone very well were making polite small talk in a very restrained way. Neither of those options was attractive to me, but Emily eventually said that we should mingle, so I did.
7362:
Transcription

Fortunately, then one of the organisers announced that we were going to play a game. We had to write down our memories and guess who had written them. You'd think it would fall flat because most people barely knew each other, but actually, it was a good ice-breaker. After that, people were no longer pretending to be interested in each others' careers and families. We knew what to talk about – you know, events, classrooms, teachers and so on, and it brought home what we had in common; and also what set us apart, because people had responded differently to what was basically the same experience.
7363:
Transcription

Later on, we had a tour, and the headteacher gave us an update on the school's facilities and the latest news. She spoke proudly of the new history block, the computer laboratories and the school's excellence and recognition in music. What struck me, though, is how little had changed. Despite all these modern updates, the school ethos is still to help teenagers excel in activities that are somewhat outdated rather than teaching the kinds of skills that are valued today.
7364:
Transcription

Naturally, that led to a discussion about what the school had done well and what it should have done differently. Interestingly, we all used to think the school was far too strict, but now I appreciate that that approach taught me discipline. I also have always thought that the school had too few options. It prepared everyone for the academic route to university, and to be fair, it did that very well. Pretty much everyone got in. But as far as preparation for the workplace goes, there was none of that. It seemed they were just passing the buck.
7365:
Transcription

Although it wasn't the best evening of my life, the reunion was a good opportunity to reflect. After all, the school taught me to be hard-working and capable, and I've always been aware of the benefits that has brought me. I'm pleased to have met up with old classmates too. It was interesting to see how our shared education has shaped everyone differently, so I'll definitely keep in touch with them. I can't say my memories of school are any more positive. It'll take more than one evening to change those, but all in all, I'm glad I went.

Lots of people dream of working in the movie industry. First of all, you have to accept that you'll constantly be scraping around for work. You might get a great job for a few months, but then that's it. I've been in the business for eight years, but even now, there's no promise of a new contract after one ends. There are loads of talented, enthusiastic and qualified people in the same position.

Well, I can't speak for the people who are high up, but if you are in a junior role, like me, you spend a lot of time standing around, waiting for something to happen. You need to be acutely aware of what's going on and ready to spring into action the moment you are needed. No one wants to be kept waiting because they can't find you.

Hello everyone, and you’re so welcome to my channel about travelling the world! Today, I’d like to speak about my trip to Mexico. In September, I arrived in Cancun for a little rest and relaxation. On the second day, I joined the travel group on a bus tour to Yucatan. In this region of Mexico, we saw the Mayan pyramids, which are extremely old. The Maya people understood astronomy and the movement of the solar system. Their pyramids were built in a way to allow the planets, moon and stars to be visible to people inside these buildings. So, that was amazing. The next day, we returned to Cancun. I went to the market, bought some fruit and vegetables, and after that, I had lunch with my friend Diego at a Mexican restaurant. He recommended tacos, which are corn shells filled with meat and a hot sauce. They were very spicy! I had to drink a lot of water. We went shopping, and I went into an old, dark store. To my surprise, I saw the most beautiful lamp, so I bought it. Unfortunately, I only stayed for four days in Mexico, which is a pity because it wasn’t enough time to see much. I recommend two weeks to really see the country!

DR. STEVENS: Absolutely... and thank you for having me. Well, I've been looking into the therapeutic effects of pets on human emotions, especially among young adults. I've always loved animals, so this study was really fun for me.

This was concerning for the school because if students didn't return in the second year, they could lose a lot of business, especially as this was a private school. INTERVIEWER: Could you explain the details of your experiment?

DR. STEVENS: Certainly. We introduced pets to all the first-year students at the start of the school year, and they had to take care of the animals from September until June. In this 'pet support' experiment, we aimed to see if having a little dog or cat would help students stay in college. If they returned for the second year, they were allowed to keep their pets. We divided the experiment into three parts: an interview at the beginning of the study to understand the well-being of the students, a second interview halfway through, and a final interview at the end.

They mentioned that having the responsibility of a dog or cat gave them a reason to come back. Overall, They felt more relaxed and happier and enjoyed school more during the year. We now realize that 'pet support' is successful. It helps people feel less lonely, more at ease in new situations, and having a pet gives them a sense of responsibility.

AIDEN: I was thirteen years old when I took a flight to London with my mum. Neither of us had been on a plane before, so we were excited but nervous. We knew that we had to get to the airport three hours before our flight took off, but what we thought was the check-in time was actually the departure time, so when we arrived at the airport, the flight was already boarding! The lady told us not to worry; we wouldn't miss our flight. But there were only two seats left, one in the middle and one at the back. We were so disappointed. I didn't want to sit away from my mum because I was nervous about flying, and she wanted to sit with me because she doesn't speak English. The lady must have seen my face because she said, 'Don't worry, I can sit you together.' She printed out our boarding cards and we ran to the gate. When we boarded, we turned towards economy class and the flight attendant told us we were going the wrong way. The lady at the desk had put us in business class so that we could sit together! PHIL: Of course. We actually have three types of walks. Our long walks aren’t that long—usually around eight miles, starting at 10 am... well, we meet half an hour before, so the walk leader can get everyone organised... and we’re usually finished at around 2, 2.30.
EMMA: I’m not sure I’m up to 8 miles yet...
